description.p: rPGP is an OpenPGP certificate manager in the spirit of KDE's Kleopatra: a window that lists your certificates and lets you generate, import, export, certify, sign, encrypt, decrypt and verify without touching a command line.

It keeps two questions apart that are easy to confuse and dangerous to mix up: whether a certificate is internally valid, and whether the name on it belongs to the person you think. The first is arithmetic; the second is the web of trust, computed from the certifications in your own store.

ul.li: Generate keys to RFC 9580 or RFC 4880, with a passphrase and a pre-made revocation certificate
Sign, encrypt, decrypt and verify files, or text in a built-in notepad
Encrypt to certificates, to a password, or to both at once
Certify identities, mark trusted introducers, and see what authenticates a key
Revoke keys, user IDs and subkeys, with the consequences spelled out
Look up and publish keys over WKD and HKPS
Use keys held on a smartcard through gpg-agent, so the secret never leaves the card

description.p: Written in Rust throughout, using Sequoia for OpenPGP and Slint for the interface. No webview, no Qt, and it never shells out to gpg.

description.p: Fixes for ways an ordinary import or edit could damage a key you hold, for file output and Copy in the Flatpak, and for reaching gpg-agent beyond Linux, plus a Windows installer.

ul.li: Importing a GnuPG export of a key you already held could replace its secret with a stub, the placeholder GnuPG writes for a key kept on a smartcard or offline. A stub no longer displaces a usable secret, and signing passes over a stub to a key that can sign
Choosing the revocation certificate of a key you hold in Import revoked the key at once and for good. rPGP now asks first, unless the same file also holds the key

Add user ID wrote a binding with no key flags and no expiry. On a key made by GnuPG that binding became the primary one, leaving the primary key unable to certify or sign, and without an expiry. The new binding is now copied from the primary user ID's

Upgrading does not repair a key damaged by any of the three above. A secret replaced by a stub comes back by importing a full secret export again. A key revoked through Import, or given a user ID that way, has to be deleted from rPGP and imported again from a backup or from GnuPG, after which Trust root needs ticking again; until then, adding another user ID copies the damage. A revocation already published cannot be withdrawn

A certificate revoked as a whole was still offered and used as a recipient, and a revoked key of your own still signed. Revoked certificates are now refused for encrypting, signing and certifying, and changing the expiry or adding a user ID no longer brings a retired key back into use

Changing a key's expiry failed outright when a subkey was on a smartcard, and skipped signing and authentication subkeys whose secret is on another machine, so they lapsed on their old date while the details pane showed the new one. Both are now renewed, as long as the primary key is on this machine

A secret key that GnuPG 2.3 or later exported with a passphrase could not decrypt, and often could not sign, when it used elliptic curves, as GnuPG's default keys do. It now unlocks, except on Brainpool curves, which this build cannot use

gpg-agent is now found on Windows with Gpg4win, on macOS when rPGP is opened from the Finder, and in the Flatpak when the host's agent is running or started by systemd. Certify is offered for a key whose primary is held only by the agent, and a message is decrypted with the agent key it was encrypted to

Windows releases add a per-user installer that puts rPGP in the Start Menu and in Apps & Features without asking for an administrator. When winget offers this version it installs that, and a 0.1.3 install from winget will not upgrade to it: with rPGP closed, uninstall jzbz.rPGP and install it again, once. Certificates and keys stay where they are

In the Flatpak, Sign / Encrypt and Decrypt reported a file that never appeared under its name. The output was left in the input's folder as a hidden .xdp- file, which upgrading does not remove, and after a decrypt that file holds the plaintext. They now ask where to save through the desktop's save dialog

Copy in the Flatpak failed on sway, and is expected to have failed on GNOME, since neither offers a sandboxed app the clipboard protocol it used. It now falls back to the standard Wayland clipboard there. The Flatpak also moves to the 26.08 freedesktop runtime

Someone holding no key that can sign could not encrypt a file, because Sign could not be unticked. A new key's passphrase is now asked for twice, so a typo in one of the two is caught before it becomes the key's
The Trust root box of an imported secret key was drawn ticked and could not be changed, while the web of trust ignored the key. It now works, so a restored backup can be made a trust root again

Control, formatting and direction-changing characters in a user ID are shown as code points, so a name can no longer rearrange the words around it. Where a key is chosen, identities that read alike are told apart by key ID

A message rPGP signs and encrypts now names its intended recipients, so when one of them encrypts it on to someone else, rPGP shows that reader a signature that is not valid. A copy passed on under a password is not caught

Key lookups no longer reach loopback, private or carrier-grade NAT addresses, whether written as an address or reached through a name that resolves to one, so a Web Key Directory inside a private network is no longer reached. The configured keyserver is exempt. A Web Key Directory reply keeps only the certificates carrying the address asked for

Lookups and publishing ignore proxy settings in the environment, so where a proxy is the only way out they stop working. Outside the Flatpak they trust the system's certificate store as well as the bundled roots. Two advisories in the HTTPS stack are fixed

A password-protected message can no longer make a decrypt spend more than 2 GiB of memory, or minutes of Argon2 hashing, before the password is even checked, and a truncated Keybox file no longer hangs Import

rPGP's own copies of a passphrase are wiped once used, and passphrase fields no longer copy or cut. What the notepad's Copy button copies is marked private for clipboard managers that honour the mark, except in the Flatpak on GNOME or sway, where the status line says so

Two rPGP windows sharing a store no longer overwrite each other's changes. The store now takes a lock when it opens, so rPGP cannot open a store on a filesystem that refuses file locks. On Linux and macOS, decrypted files are created readable by their owner only

Dialogs and the certificate list work from the keyboard, apart from ticking recipients and user IDs. A disabled button can no longer be pressed through a screen reader, and the window stays responsive while a large store reloads

description.p: A way to read signatures from certificates too old for the standard policy, and fixes to what the verification banner manages to say.

ul.li: Keys certified before about 2010 sign themselves with SHA-1, so rPGP found no valid identity and no valid subkey on them and showed the whole certificate as unusable — accurate, and no help to someone trying to check a signature a project still publishes. Such a certificate now offers to accept SHA-1 from that one certificate

Accepting it widens what can be checked and nothing else. The certificate still cannot be authenticated through the web of trust, act as a trust root, vouch for another key, or be encrypted to, and every other certificate is judged exactly as strictly as before in the same operation

What comes back is not a guarantee, and says so. SHA-1 collisions are practical, so a signature that checks out shows the signer's key was involved rather than that its holder approved the document. The result leads with that, ahead of the identity verdict, and the signature is marked SHA-1 wherever it is listed
The offer appears only where it would help — where SHA-1 is the reason the certificate is unusable, not on one that is broken some other way

The reason a verification failed could be cut off in the decrypt and verify banner, sliced along the top and bottom of a box built for a single line. The longer the failure, the less of it survived, which is backwards for the message that most needs reading
That banner counted every wrapped line as one, so a verdict running to three lines was drawn outside its coloured box entirely. It is now sized to the text it actually draws
A certificate list that loads while part of the store cannot be read now names the part that failed, rather than leaving a badge missing with no explanation

description.p: A Windows build, and fixes from a second review of the whole tree plus the first end-to-end testing on each platform.

ul.li: rPGP now runs on Windows
Signing text that ended without a proper line ending produced a signature rPGP itself then called invalid. Text copied from a Windows application and trimmed of its last blank line did exactly that

A certificate revoked twice showed the most recent reason rather than the most serious, so a later "no longer used" could hide "the secret key may be compromised" — which anyone holding the stolen key could arrange
Certifying an identity its owner had revoked is now refused. A revoked address is one the holder has disowned, and often one the provider has since given to somebody else
The expiry of a key imported from GnuPG could not be changed at all. Keys with an authentication subkey, which is what GnuPG makes, failed the whole operation
A message that was signed but never encrypted was reported as decrypted, telling the reader that something which crossed the network in clear had arrived confidentially
Importing a file that held part of a key you already had could discard the material you held. The two are now merged
A certification is attributed only after it verifies, so a packet naming your key without being signed by it can no longer appear in the list as yours
Verified badges belong to an identity rather than to the whole certificate, so an unauthenticated name on a key can no longer inherit another identity's verdict
A screen reader can now see which recipients are selected, and every dropdown says what it is for
Toolbar buttons no longer overlap when the window is narrow
A failure to open the certificate store now says so, instead of the app starting and vanishing without a word
An oversized or padded message is refused rather than allowed to exhaust memory or CPU

description.p: Fixes found by a security and optimization review of the whole tree.

ul.li: Decrypting a file could destroy an unrelated file that happened to sit at the name used for the temporary output

A secret key that arrived by import silently became a web-of-trust root, so an imported key could make identities it had certified read as verified. Keys you generate are still roots; an imported one can be made one from its details pane
Certifying an identity could be silently prevented by a planted revocation packet that named your key without being signed by it
Publishing reported success when the confirmation-mail request had failed, leaving an address the keyserver would never serve
Keyserver lookups no longer follow redirects to private addresses
The interface font is bundled, so the app looks the same however it is installed
Reloading a large keyring is roughly twice as fast
